facts.text: Since 1950 the main land-use change in Costa Rica has been turning forest into pasture and farmland, as growth was tied to farm exports and cattle ranching.
In the 1970s and 1980s, few countries on Earth were clearing their forests as fast as Costa Rica was.
In the 1980s economic reforms made farming and cattle ranching on marginal forest land less profitable.
Forests benefited when support for farming and ranching shrank and meat prices fell; secondary forests grew back on abandoned pastures.
Forest Law 7575 of 1996 recognized four services of forests: carbon storage, water protection, biodiversity and scenic beauty.
Under the law, Costa Rica pays landowners for forest conservation, reforestation and agroforestry through its payments for environmental services program.
A fuel tax passed with the 1996 forest law is the main source of money for the payments.
By October 2005 about 250,000 hectares were under contract, 95 percent of it natural forest under conservation.
The program depended heavily on the fuel tax and on short-term donor financing.
Plantations and secondary forests have less environmental value than the natural forests that were lost.
The World Bank describes Costa Rica as the first tropical country to reverse deforestation; forests now cover close to 60 percent of the country.
Costa Rica received the UN Champion of the Earth award in 2019.
In 2022 Costa Rica became the first Latin American country paid by the World Bank's Forest Carbon Partnership Facility for reducing forest emissions, receiving 16.4 million US dollars.
